At the edge of evening, the city changes its mind.

All day it insists on being useful: buses arrive, doors open, people cross streets with their thoughts held tight. Then the sun slips behind the rooftops, and usefulness loosens. A window glows. Someone waters a plant. A dog takes its time sniffing the same patch of pavement it inspected yesterday.

Nothing important has happened, and yet the day feels complete.

Maybe that is one of the quiet miracles: the world does not always ask us to become someone else. Sometimes it only asks us to notice where we are—the warm cup between our hands, the distant sound of a train, the last gold light caught on a brick wall—and to let that be enough for a while.
